articles.title: Verify before you run
articles.excerpt: You know the workflow. You describe the task, the AI writes the PowerShell, it looks right, you run it. Most days this works fine. Then September happened. A story went around about an rmdir suggested…
articles.body: You know the workflow. You describe the task, the AI writes the PowerShell, it looks right, you run it. Most days this works fine. Then September happened. A story went around about an rmdir suggested by AI landing in the wrong place, and a drive disappearing. Generation is a solved problem now. Verification is the part most of us skip. Here is the pass I run before any script written by AI touches a production box. It takes about five minutes. First, read every destructive cmdlet. Search the script for Remove, Stop, Set, Clear, Disable, and Format. For each hit, ask one question: if this runs against the wrong scope, what breaks? AI is confident about syntax and careless about scope. A Remove ADUser with a bad filter is a resume event. Second, run it with WhatIf. It is free information.

articles.title: What a health startup actually has to build before its first feature (and what you can skip)
articles.excerpt: Every health app starts the same way. You have an idea (a symptom tracker, an AI assistant for lab results, a remote-monitoring dashboard), and before you can ship the first screen that matters, you a…
articles.body: Every health app starts the same way. You have an idea (a symptom tracker, an AI assistant for lab results, a remote-monitoring dashboard), and before you can ship the first screen that matters, you are designing a database for “a patient’s medical record”. That is where months go. Here is the list we kept running into, and what we decided you should not have to build yourself. The invisible backlog. Before the first real feature, a health product needs: A data model for medical records (measurements, labs, conditions, medications, documents, with units, reference ranges and real measurement dates). Standard codes: LOINC, ICD-10, ATC. An API and its docs. Patient-authorized access: consent that expires, can be revoked, and is visible to the person.

articles.title: Realtime Notification Preferences Testing — Stock Trading Watchlists Without Flaky Timing
articles.excerpt: Short answer: test a realtime stock trading watchlist with a deterministic event log, a controllable clock, and an explicit reconnect cursor; never make the assertion wait for a wall-clock delay and h…
articles.body: Short answer: test a realtime stock trading watchlist with a deterministic event log, a controllable clock, and an explicit reconnect cursor; never make the assertion wait for a wall-clock delay and hope a notification arrives. The deciding constraint is recovery, not raw delivery speed. A watchlist can look correct on a clean connection and still duplicate, omit, or misroute an update after a preference change and reconnect. The same failure boundary appears in a healthtech dashboard that streams device status: a disconnected clinician's screen must resume from a known position, while the preference snapshot used for each notification remains explainable. This is an architecture decision record for that boundary.

articles.excerpt: Astronomers have used NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to break down the cause of a remarkable formation of radio waves they have nicknamed the “Treble Clef” because its distinct shape strongly resemb…
articles.body: X-ray: NASA/CXC/INAF-IRA/A. Botteon et al.; Infrared: UKIDSS-GPS ; Radio: ASTRON/LOFAR; Image processing: NASA/CXC/SAO/N. Wolk Astronomers have used NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to break down the cause of a remarkable formation of radio waves they have nicknamed the “Treble Clef” because its distinct shape strongly resembles the musical symbol. The researchers discovered the Treble Clef is likely caused by an outburst from a supermassive black hole, followed by a collision of two galaxy clusters. A paper describing the findings, led by Andrea Botteon of the National Institute for Astrophysics, or INAF, in Italy, published Wednesday in the Astronomy & Astrophysics journal .

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 14, 1947: Test pilot Chuck Yeager breaks the sound barrier in the Bell X-1, the first X-plane
articles.excerpt: On this day in space! Oct. 14, 1947: Test pilot Chuck Yeager breaks the sound barrier in the Bell X-1, the first X-plane
articles.body: On Oct. 14, 1947, Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier for the first time! Chuck Yeager was a test pilot for the U.S. Air Force who made history by flying an aircraft faster than the speed of sound. Yeager made his historic flight in a Bell X-1 rocket plane that he named "Glamorous Glennis" after his wife. Yeager had broken two ribs the night before when he fell off a horse, but that didn't stop him! His aircraft was dropped from a Boeing B-29 bomber before accelerating to a speed of Mach 1.07, which is about 821 mph (1,321 km/h). The speed of sound, Mach 1, is about 760 mph (1,223 km/h). USAF Capt. Charles E. Yeager (shown standing with the Bell X-1 supersonic rocket plane) became the first man to fly faster than the speed of sound in level flight on Oct. 14, 1947.

articles.body: Don't expect any of the Artemis II moon astronauts to fly again soon. On Tuesday (Oct. 13), NASA announced that Artemis II mission specialist Christina Koch will become the agency’s acting deputy chief engineer, effective Nov. 1. "With this appointment, Koch will transition to management astronaut status and will no longer be eligible for future spaceflight assignments," NASA officials wrote in a statement on Tuesday . Her three Artemis II crewmates had already shared their next moves, none of which put another spaceflight in play in the near future. Mission commander Reid Wiseman and pilot Victor Glover , both of NASA, became "emeritus" astronauts last month, a role that seems to include planning, advising and mentoring duties but no flights into the final frontier.

articles.title: NASA’s Space X CRS-35 Launch Jellyfish
articles.excerpt: Sunlight illuminates the exhaust plumes of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carrying the company’s Dragon spacecraft on Oct. 13, 2026. This visual phenomenon is known as a “jellyfish”; it happens near sunrise…
articles.body: NASA/John Kraus Sunlight illuminates the exhaust plumes of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carrying the company’s Dragon spacecraft on Oct. 13, 2026. This visual phenomenon is known as a “jellyfish”; it happens near sunrise or sunset when the exhaust plume from the rocket becomes brightly illuminated, creating a glowing shape resembling a jellyfish. The mission lifted off at 6:33 a.m. EDT from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, carrying scientific investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station on SpaceX’s 35th commercial resupply services mission for NASA. The rocket’s exhaust plumes were visible across the eastern United States.

articles.title: 'The X-Files' is officially returning as Hulu picks up Ryan Coogler's 'reimagining' of the sci-fi icon
articles.excerpt: Trust no one.
articles.body: The truth is once again out there, as Disney & Hulu confirmed today that they have picked up a new "The X-Files" show for a full season. Described as a "reimagining" of the classic series, the project comes from Ryan Coogler, the acclaimed writer and director of "Creed", "Black Panther", and "Sinners", and will star Danielle Deadwyler and Himesh Patel. The show's premise will sound very familiar to fans of the original, as it centers on "two highly decorated but vastly different FBI agents who form an unlikely bond when they are assigned to a long-shuttered division devoted to cases involving unexplained phenomena." "I've loved 'The X-Files' for a long time, so getting the chance to write and direct the pilot has meant a great deal to me," said Coogler.

articles.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
articles.excerpt: "Small weight-based replicators" could usher in a new generation of computer worms.
articles.body: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet-of-things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered.
